MSK__Joint Pain:
Joint pain (arthralgia) is one of the commonest presenting symptoms — and the trick is a structured sort before you reach for tests. Ask four questions:
  • (1) Articular or periarticular? — is the joint itself painful (pain on all movement, effusion, deep/diffuse) or a tendon / bursa / bone around it (point tenderness, pain on one movement)?
  • (2) Inflammatory or mechanical? — inflammatory = early-morning stiffness >30–60 min, eases with use, swelling / warmth / erythema, night pain, systemic upset; mechanical / degenerative = worse through the day / with use, stiffness <30 min, better with rest.
  • (3) What pattern? — mono (1) vs oligo (2–4) vs poly (≥5), symmetry, large vs small, axial vs peripheral, migratory vs additive (see monoarthritis, polyarthritis).
  • (4) Acute or chronic?
🚨A single acute hot, swollen, painful joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — aspirate the joint (before antibiotics if possible) and do not delay (see hot swollen joint, bone & joint infection). Also flagged: fever with systemic upset, joint pain with a rash / photosensitivity, oral ulcers or red eye (connective tissue disease / spondyloarthropathy), new inflammatory arthritis with weight loss or night sweats (malignancy / vasculitis), and any joint pain after trauma (fracture).

1Recognise & sort
🔍Take the pain apart
  • Articular (pain on all movement, effusion) vs periarticular (point tenderness, pain on one specific movement — tendon / bursa)
  • Inflammatory (morning stiffness >30–60 min, eases with use, hot / swollen, night pain) vs mechanical (worse with use, stiffness <30 min, eases with rest)
  • Define onset (acute vs chronic), number of joints, symmetry, and whether it is migratory or additive
🚩Red-flag patterns
  • Single acute hot swollen joint → septic arthritis until proven otherwise — aspirate (see joint infection)
  • Fever / systemic upset, or arthritis with a rash, oral ulcers, red eye or new murmur (CTD, spondyloarthropathy, endocarditis)
  • New inflammatory arthritis + weight loss / night sweats (malignancy / vasculitis); any post-traumatic joint pain (fracture)
🔵Acute patterns
  • Acute monoarthritis: septic arthritis, gout / pseudogout (see crystal arthropathy), haemarthrosis, trauma
  • Migratory (moves joint to joint): gonococcal, rheumatic fever, viral, Lyme, early connective tissue disease
  • Acute symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis: viral (e.g. parvovirus), early rheumatoid arthritis
🟢Chronic patterns
  • Symmetrical small joints (MCP / PIP / wrist), morning stiffness → rheumatoid arthritis (see RA)
  • Asymmetrical large joints / axial + enthesitis / dactylitis → spondyloarthropathy (psoriatic, reactive, axial, IBD-related, see spondyloarthropathy)
  • DIP + weight-bearing joints, worse with use, bony swelling → osteoarthritis (see OA)
🟣Don’t-miss systemic clues
  • Photosensitive rash, oral ulcers, Raynaud’s, serositis → connective tissue disease / SLE (see CTD)
  • Psoriasis / nail changes, uveitis, urethritis or recent diarrhoea, IBD → a spondyloarthropathy
  • Widespread pain, tender points, fatigue, non-inflammatory → fibromyalgia (a diagnosis of exclusion, see fibromyalgia)
  • Over-50s, proximal shoulder / pelvic-girdle pain + long morning stiffness, very high ESR → polymyalgia rheumatica (watch for giant cell arteritis)
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Examine with look–feel–move: effusion, warmth, deformity, range; screen the other joints, skin, nails and eyes
  • Bloods: FBC, CRP / ESR, urate, RF & anti-CCP, ANA, HLA-B27 (selectively), U&E / LFTs
  • Joint aspiration (MC&S, crystals, Gram — mandatory for a hot joint) and imaging (X-ray, ultrasound / MRI) as guided
Sort before you test. Two questions do most of the work: is it inflammatory or mechanical (the morning-stiffness clock — >30–60 min and easing with use = inflammatory), and how many joints, how symmetrical? Those two axes place most arthritis before a single blood test — and a single hot joint always gets aspirated to exclude sepsis.

MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint:
An acute hot, swollen, painful joint carries one overriding rule: it is septic arthritis until proven otherwise.
  • Untreated septic arthritis destroys the joint within days and carries a real mortality, so the priority is a diagnostic joint aspiration before you commit to any other label.
  • The differential is short and worth knowing cold: septic arthritis, crystal arthritis (gout / pseudogout), haemarthrosis (trauma / anticoagulation / bleeding disorder), a reactive arthritis, an acute flare of a known inflammatory arthritis, and trauma / fracture.
  • The one test that separates them is the synovial fluid — Gram stain, culture, cell count and crystals (see joint pain, bone & joint infection).
🚨Aspirate the joint URGENTLY, before antibiotics — send fluid for Gram stain, culture, cell count and crystals, take blood cultures, then start empirical IV antibiotics and refer for washout (see septic arthritis). Never dismiss a hot joint as “just a gout flare” — sepsis and crystals can coexist. A prosthetic joint must not be tapped at the bedside — refer to orthopaedics for aspiration in theatre.

1Recognise & act
🔍Recognise it
  • Red, hot, swollen, exquisitely tender joint with an effusion, markedly reduced range and held still
  • Ask about fever / systemic upset, speed of onset, prior joint disease, trauma and anticoagulation
  • Note risk factors for sepsis: prosthetic joint, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, immunosuppression, IVDU, a skin breach
🚩The emergency response
  • Septic arthritis until proven otherwise → URGENT aspiration before antibiotics (Gram / culture / crystals / cell count)
  • Take blood cultures + FBC / CRP, then start empirical IV antibiotics and refer for joint washout (see joint infection)
  • Prosthetic joint → do not aspirate at the bedside; refer to orthopaedics for theatre aspiration
🔵The differential
  • Septic arthritis: Staph aureus commonest; gonococcal in the young / sexually active (migratory, tenosynovitis, pustules)
  • Crystal arthritis: gout (podagra, see gouty tophi) and pseudogout (CPPD, knee / wrist, elderly, see crystal arthropathy)
  • Haemarthrosis (trauma, anticoagulation, haemophilia), reactive arthritis, and an acute flare of RA / spondyloarthropathy (see RA)
🟢Read the synovial fluid
  • Septic: turbid / purulent, very high WCC (often >50×10⁹/L, >90% neutrophils), organisms on Gram / culture
  • Crystal: negatively birefringent needles = urate (gout); positively birefringent rhomboids = CPPD (pseudogout)
  • Haemarthrosis: frank blood (± fat globules if intra-articular fracture)
🟣Mimics & pitfalls
  • Cellulitis / bursitis can look similar but the joint moves freely and the effusion is outside the joint line
  • A hot swollen foot in a diabetic may be a Charcot (neuropathic) joint, not infection (see neuropathic foot, Charcot joint)
  • Serum urate is often normal or low during an acute gout attack — it does not exclude gout, and a raised urate does not confirm it
🩺Investigate & treat
  • Joint aspiration (the decisive test) + blood cultures, FBC, CRP / ESR, urate, U&E, coagulation
  • Empirical IV antibiotics after aspiration (per local policy, e.g. flucloxacillin) and surgical washout / drainage
  • In a child with a hot hip use the Kocher criteria (non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5°C, ESR >40, WCC >12) to weigh septic vs transient synovitis
Tap first, label later. Every acute hot swollen joint is septic until the aspirate says otherwise — so the reflex is arthrocentesis before antibiotics, blood cultures, then empirical IV cover and washout. Gout is the commonest true cause, but you can only call it gout after excluding sepsis, because the two can sit in the same joint.

MSK__Monoarthritis:
Monoarthritis is inflammation of a single joint. The first split is tempo.
  • An acute monoarthritis (days) is a medical emergency — septic arthritis until proven otherwise — and is worked up as a hot joint (see acute hot swollen joint): septic, crystal (gout / pseudogout), haemarthrosis, reactive or traumatic.
  • A chronic monoarthritis (persisting >6 weeks) opens a different differential that is easy to forget: osteoarthritis, chronic infection (tuberculosis, fungal, Brucella), a monoarticular presentation of RA / a spondyloarthropathy, pigmented villonodular synovitis, tumour, or avascular necrosis.
  • The unifying move is the same: aspirate the joint — and if it stays undiagnosed, biopsy the synovium (see joint pain).
🚨Any acute monoarthritis is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — aspirate before antibiotics, take blood cultures, and treat (see septic arthritis). Do not be reassured by a “normal” serum urate. For a chronic monoarthritis that resists diagnosis, think tuberculosis and tumour — both need a synovial (or bone) biopsy, not just more blood tests. A hot swollen foot in a diabetic may be a Charcot joint, not sepsis.

  • Crystal: gout (podagra, see gouty tophi) and pseudogout (CPPD, knee / wrist, elderly, see crystal arthropathy)
  • Haemarthrosis (trauma, anticoagulation, haemophilia), reactive arthritis, trauma / internal derangement
🟢Chronic monoarthritis (>6 weeks)
  • Osteoarthritis (commonest chronic mono, see OA) and avascular necrosis (see AVN)
  • Chronic infection: tuberculosis, fungal, Brucella, Lyme — indolent, needs synovial biopsy / culture

  • Imaging (X-ray, ultrasound, MRI); if a chronic mono stays undiagnosed → synovial biopsy (TB, PVNS, tumour)
Tempo picks the differential. Acute monoarthritis is a hot-joint emergency (septic until proven otherwise); chronic monoarthritis (>6 weeks) is a different list topped by osteoarthritis, TB and tumour. Both start with a joint aspiration — and the chronic, undiagnosed joint ends with a synovial biopsy.

MSK__Polyarthritis:
Polyarthritis is arthritis of five or more joints (2–4 joints is an oligoarthritis). Unlike a single hot joint, the diagnosis here is made by pattern recognition along a few axes:
  • Symmetry — symmetrical small-joint disease (RA, viral, lupus) versus asymmetrical large-joint ± spinal disease (the spondyloarthropathies).
  • Joint size — small hand joints vs large weight-bearing joints.
  • Course over time — additive (RA), migratory / flitting (rheumatic fever, gonococcus, Lyme), or intermittent (palindromic rheumatism, gout).
  • Deciding whether the process is inflammatory (early-morning stiffness >30 min, swelling, raised CRP) or non-inflammatory (osteoarthritis) frames everything (see joint pain, monoarthritis).
🚨A polyarthritis is rarely the same emergency as a single hot joint, but do not miss: an acutely septic joint superimposed on a polyarthritis (one joint far angrier than the rest → aspirate it), gonococcal / meningococcal arthritis-dermatitis in the young, and a systemic vasculitis or connective-tissue disease with organ involvement (see vasculitis, connective tissue disease). Early rheumatoid arthritis needs urgent rheumatology referral — a “treat-to-target” window exists before erosions form.

🔍Count & classify
  • ≥5 joints = polyarthritis; 2–4 = oligoarthritis; 1 = monoarthritis (see monoarthritis)
  • Decide inflammatory (morning stiffness >30 min, swelling, high CRP / ESR) vs non-inflammatory (OA)

🔵Symmetry & size
  • Symmetrical small joints (MCP / PIP / wrists) → rheumatoid arthritis, viral, lupus
  • Asymmetrical large joints ± spine / DIP → seronegative spondyloarthropathy (see spondyloarthropathy)
  • DIP + Heberden nodes, older, non-inflammatory → osteoarthritis (see OA)
🟢Course over time
  • Additive (joints accumulate and stay) → rheumatoid arthritis (see RA)
  • Migratory / flitting (moves from joint to joint) → rheumatic fever, gonococcal, Lyme (see Lyme disease)
  • Intermittent / self-limiting → palindromic rheumatism, viral, polyarticular gout (see crystal arthropathy)
🟣Look outside the joints
  • Skin: psoriasis, malar / vasculitic rash, tophi, nail pitting; eyes: uveitis, dry eyes; mucosa: ulcers
  • Systemic: fever + salmon rash + sore throat → adult-onset Still’s (see Still's disease); Raynaud’s, sicca → CTD
  • Preceding trigger: sore throat (rheumatic fever), diarrhoea / urethritis (reactive), a viral prodrome (parvovirus B19)
🩺Investigate by pattern
  • Inflammatory markers (CRP / ESR), RF and anti-CCP (RA), ANA → ENA / complement (lupus / CTD)
  • Viral serology (parvovirus B19, hepatitis B / C), urate, HLA-B27 selectively, ASOT if rheumatic fever
  • X-rays of hands / feet (erosions in RA / psoriatic; normal in viral / lupus) — and aspirate any disproportionately hot joint
🚩Don’t-miss patterns
  • One joint far angrier than the rest → superimposed septic arthritis — aspirate it (see joint infection)
  • Young + migratory arthritis + pustules / tenosynovitis → disseminated gonococcus
  • Arthritis + rash + renal / lung / neuro signs → vasculitis or connective-tissue disease — look for organ involvement
Pattern beats the single joint. For many joints, ask four questions — how many, how symmetrical, what size, and what course — and the differential falls out. Symmetrical small-joint + additive is rheumatoid until proven otherwise; asymmetrical large-joint + axial is a spondyloarthropathy; migratory flags rheumatic fever, gonococcus and Lyme.

MSK__Back Pain:
Back pain is one of the commonest presentations in medicine and the great majority is mechanical — benign, movement-related and self-limiting. The entire skill is a triage:
  • Sort each patient into mechanical, inflammatory, or “red-flag” serious pathology.
  • Screen actively for the emergencies you cannot miss — cauda equina syndrome, malignancy / metastasis, infection (discitis / epidural abscess), fracture, and a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm (see lower back & spine).
  • Always remember pain referred from a viscus (aorta, pancreas, kidney, peptic ulcer).
  • Simple mechanical pain does not need imaging; a red flag needs it urgently (see joint pain).
🚨Cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency. Saddle anaesthesia, bilateral sciatica, urinary retention with overflow, faecal incontinence or reduced anal tone → immediate whole-spine MRI and surgical decompression — delay causes permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction (see cauda equina / spine). A leaking AAA can present as sudden back pain with collapse — feel for a pulsatile mass (see AAA). Thoracic back pain, night pain and systemic upset should always raise malignancy or infection.

MSK__Neck Pain:
Neck pain, like back pain, is usually mechanical — cervical spondylosis, muscular strain or whiplash — and settles with time. The exam skill is the same triage:
  • Separate benign mechanical pain from a cervical radiculopathy (nerve root), the can’t-miss cervical myelopathy (spinal-cord compression), and true red-flag pathology — infection, malignancy, fracture and rheumatoid atlanto-axial subluxation.
  • Remember the neck is a site of referred and dangerous pain: meningitis (meningism, see neck stiffness), cardiac pain to the jaw / neck, and carotid or vertebral artery dissection.
  • The single most important pattern to learn is myelopathy, because it is easily missed and needs surgery (see spinal cord disorders, back pain).
🚨Cervical myelopathy is the neck’s cauda equina. Progressive gait disturbance, clumsy hands, Lhermitte’s phenomenon and upper-motor-neurone signs in the legs (brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars, Hoffmann’s) → urgent cervical-spine MRI and spinal referral (see cervical myelopathy). In rheumatoid arthritis, atlanto-axial subluxation can compress the cord — especially dangerous during neck manipulation or intubation (see rheumatoid arthritis). After trauma, immobilise and apply the Canadian C-spine rule; fever + neck stiffness + photophobia is meningitis, not a stiff neck.

MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (Myopathy:
Muscle weakness means a true loss of power — which must first be separated from its common mimics: pain-limited “weakness” (arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica) and generalised fatigue / asthenia.
  • Once you have true weakness, localise the lesion: is it the muscle (a myopathy — proximal, symmetric, no sensory loss, high CK), the nerve (distal, with sensory signs), the neuromuscular junction (fatigable, ocular / bulbar), or the central / UMN pathway (see weakness — localisation)?
  • This topic follows the myopathy arm — where the key emergencies are inflammatory myositis with breathing / swallowing involvement, an underlying malignancy in dermatomyositis, and rhabdomyolysis.
🚨Rhabdomyolysis (muscle pain + dark urine + very high CK) causes acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia — check CK, U&E and an ECG, and give aggressive IV fluids. Inflammatory myositis that reaches the pharyngeal muscles (dysphagia / aspiration) or the respiratory muscles is an emergency (see inflammatory myositis). Dermatomyositis in an adult is paraneoplastic until proven otherwise — screen for an underlying cancer. A myasthenic crisis (fatigable bulbar / respiratory weakness) needs airway support (see neuromuscular junction disorders).

🔍Is it TRUE weakness?
  • True weakness = reduced power on formal testing; pain-limited effort (arthritis, PMR) and fatigue are the mimics (see PMR / vasculitis)
  • Polymyalgia rheumatica: proximal stiffness & pain, age >50, high ESR, but strength is normal
  • Ask about the functional task: rising from a chair, climbing stairs, combing hair (proximal) vs fine hand tasks / tripping (distal)
🔵Localise the lesion
  • Myopathy (muscle): proximal, symmetric, no sensory loss, reflexes preserved until late, CK raised
  • Neuropathy (nerve): distal, with sensory signs and wasting, reduced reflexes (see foot drop)
  • NMJ: fatigable, ocular / bulbar, no sensory loss, normal CK (myasthenia, see NMJ disorders); UMN / central → see weakness
🟢Causes of a myopathy
  • Inflammatory: polymyositis and dermatomyositis (rash + weakness), inclusion-body myositis (see myositis)
  • Drug / toxic: statins and alcohol (raised CK), long-term steroids (steroid myopathy, typically normal CK); endocrine: thyroid disease, Cushing’s, osteomalacia
  • Inherited: muscular dystrophies (e.g. Duchenne, myotonic) and metabolic myopathies (see muscular dystrophies)
🟣Spot dermatomyositis
  • Heliotrope rash (violaceous lids), Gottron’s papules (knuckles), shawl / V sign, nailfold changes
  • Proximal weakness + these skin signs = dermatomyositis — screen for underlying malignancy in adults
  • Polymyositis is the same weakness without the rash (see connective tissue disease)
🚩Red flags
  • Rhabdomyolysis: muscle pain + dark (tea-coloured) urine + very high CK → AKI + hyperkalaemia; fluids + ECG
  • Bulbar / respiratory myositis: dysphagia, aspiration, weak cough / breathing — monitor FVC
  • Myasthenic crisis: worsening fatigable bulbar / respiratory weakness → airway & ITU support (see NMJ)
🩺Investigate
  • CK (very high in myositis / rhabdomyolysis; mildly raised in many dystrophies but very high in Duchenne / Becker), U&E, TFTs, ESR / CRP, calcium
  • Autoantibodies: ANA, anti-Jo-1 (antisynthetase), anti-Mi-2; EMG and muscle biopsy for inflammatory myopathy
  • Malignancy screen in dermatomyositis; anti-AChR / anti-MuSK antibodies if NMJ suspected

MSK__Bone Pain:
Bone pain arises from the bone itself — a deep, boring, often unremitting ache that is classically worse at night and not simply movement-related (which distinguishes it from joint or muscle pain).
  • The dominant concern is malignancy: in an older adult, metastasis (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid) and myeloma; in a young patient, a primary bone tumour (osteosarcoma, Ewing’s).
  • The rest of the list is metabolic (osteomalacia, Paget’s, hyperparathyroidism), infective (osteomyelitis), traumatic / pathological fracture, avascular necrosis and sickle-cell infarction.
  • Two tools do most of the work: the bone profile (calcium, phosphate, ALP) and a plain X-ray (lytic vs sclerotic).
🚨Bone pain with night pain, rest pain, weight loss or a past cancer is malignancy until proven otherwise. In an older adult think metastasis and myeloma — check calcium (hypercalcaemia), a myeloma screen and PSA, and image (see bone tumours, myeloma). A pathological fracture through abnormal bone, and malignant spinal-cord / cauda equina compression, are the emergencies (see back pain). Fever + focal bone pain is osteomyelitis until proven otherwise (see bone & joint infection).

🔍Recognise bone pain
  • Deep, boring, unremitting ache, often worse at night and not purely movement-related
  • Distinguish from joint pain (see joint pain) and muscle pain; localise to a bone / region and check for a mass or tenderness
  • Ask the malignancy red flags: night / rest pain, weight loss, past cancer, age
🚩Malignancy — the fear
  • Metastasis (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid) — the commonest bone malignancy in adults (see bone tumours)
  • Myeloma: bone pain + hypercalcaemia + renal impairment + anaemia (CRAB), lytic lesions (see myeloma)
  • Primary bone tumour in the young: osteosarcoma (around the knee), Ewing’s — night pain + a mass
🟢Metabolic bone disease
  • Osteomalacia: diffuse bone pain + proximal myopathy, low vitamin D, low Ca / phosphate, high ALP (see muscle weakness)
  • Paget’s disease: bone pain, deformity / warmth, isolated very high ALP with normal calcium (see metabolic bone disease)
  • Hyperparathyroidism: high Ca, bone pain (“stones, bones, groans”), osteitis fibrosa cystica
🟣Infection, fracture & infarct
  • Osteomyelitis: fever + focal bone pain / tenderness; Staph aureus, or Salmonella in sickle cell (see bone infection)
  • Fracture: traumatic, stress (athlete), or pathological through tumour / osteoporotic bone
  • Avascular necrosis (see AVN) and sickle-cell bone infarction / crisis

  • High ALP + normal Ca + deformity / warmth → Paget’s; high ALP + low Ca / phosphate + myopathy → osteomalacia
  • High calcium + bone pain → myeloma, bony metastasis or hyperparathyroidism
  • Remember osteoporosis is painless until it fractures — pain means a fracture or another diagnosis

  • Bone profile (Ca, phosphate, ALP), PTH, vitamin D, FBC / ESR, PSA, myeloma screen (electrophoresis / light chains)
  • Plain X-ray (lytic vs sclerotic, periosteal reaction); isotope bone scan for metastases; MRI for cord / marrow / primary tumour

A deep, night-time bone ache in an older adult means metastasis or myeloma until the calcium, myeloma screen, PSA and X-ray say otherwise; in a young patient with night pain and a mass, think primary bone tumour. MSK__Shoulder Pain:
Shoulder pain is common and mostly arises from the rotator cuff / subacromial space (impingement, tendinopathy, tears) or the joints (glenohumeral, acromioclavicular). Two exam habits sort it:
  • (1) Shoulder or referred? — does moving the shoulder reproduce the pain (intrinsic), or is the shoulder exam normal and the pain driven by the neck, heart, diaphragm or lung apex (referred)?
  • (2) Active vs passive movement — a rotator-cuff problem loses active movement but keeps passive range; a capsular problem (frozen shoulder or glenohumeral OA) loses both, with external rotation worst.
  • Then the painful arc localises the lesion (see shoulder disorders, neck pain).
  • The pattern that saves lives is remembering that the shoulder is a classic site of referred serious disease.
🚨A normal-looking shoulder can hide an emergency. Exertional pain in the left shoulder / arm that eases with rest is cardiac until proven otherwise → ECG + troponin (see acute coronary syndrome). Tip-of-shoulder pain from diaphragmatic irritation (Kehr’s sign) with abdominal pain or shock means ruptured spleen or ruptured ectopic — a surgical / gynae emergency. Shoulder pain + Horner’s + wasting of the small hand muscles in a smoker is a Pancoast (apical lung) tumour (see lung cancer, Horner’s). A hot, red shoulder in an unwell patient who refuses all movement is septic arthritis → aspirate (see hot swollen joint); after trauma, exclude fracture / dislocation and the acute massive cuff tear (drop-arm).

MSK__Hip Pain:
Hip pain starts with a question of site, because “hip” means different things.
  • True hip-joint pain is felt in the groin and radiates to the knee.
  • Lateral pain over the greater trochanter is greater trochanteric pain syndrome (gluteal tendinopathy / bursitis, see bursitis).
  • Buttock / posterior pain is usually referred from the lumbar spine or sacroiliac joint (see back pain).
  • The second question is age. In children, hip pathology classically presents as a limp or referred knee pain — septic hip, transient synovitis, Perthes and SUFE (see paediatric orthopaedics, limp in a child).
  • In adults think osteoarthritis, fracture, avascular necrosis and referred pain. The earliest sign of hip-joint disease is loss of internal rotation.
🚨Some hips are emergencies. A hot hip in an unwell patient who will not bear weight is septic arthritis (native or prosthetic) → urgent aspiration before antibiotics (see joint infection, hot swollen joint). In the elderly after a fall, a shortened and externally rotated leg is a neck-of-femur fracture until proven otherwise (see NOF fracture, lower limb fractures). In an adolescent — especially obese — with groin or knee pain and an externally rotated, shortened leg, think SUFE; keep them non-weight-bearing and get a frog-leg lateral X-ray (see SUFE). Never dismiss a child’s knee pain — it may be the hip. And rest / night pain with weight loss is malignancy until excluded (see bone tumours).

MSK__Knee Pain:
Knee pain is sorted by two questions:
  • (1) Was there trauma? A twist or blow points to the ligaments (ACL, PCL, collaterals), a meniscus or a fracture; an atraumatic hot swollen knee is septic or crystal arthritis until proven otherwise (see hot swollen joint).
  • (2) Where and how old? — anterior pain is patellofemoral / extensor, medial / lateral follows the compartment or collateral, posterior suggests a Baker’s cyst (see Baker’s cyst); older knees are osteoarthritis, young ones patellofemoral pain, sport injuries and, in adolescents, Osgood–Schlatter (see paediatric orthopaedics).
  • Two habits save you: aspirate every hot knee, and remember the knee is a classic site of referred hip pain — always examine the hip (see hip pain).
🚨Some knees can’t wait. A hot, swollen, red knee that the patient will not move is septic arthritis → aspirate before antibiotics (see joint infection). Inability to perform a straight-leg raise after an injury is an extensor-mechanism rupture (patellar / quadriceps tendon or patella fracture) — needs surgery. A locked knee that will not fully extend is a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear. After trauma, apply the Ottawa knee rules and exclude tibial-plateau or patellar fracture (see lower limb fractures). A painful swollen calf can be a ruptured Baker’s cyst or a DVT — do not miss the clot (see DVT, swollen leg). And in a child, knee pain may be the hip (Perthes / SUFE).

1Characterise & age-sort
🔍Characterise the gait
  • Antalgic (painful): shortened stance phase on the affected leg — points to a painful cause
  • Trendelenburg (pelvis drops to the opposite side on standing on the affected leg): weak hip abductors / hip pathology
  • Then screen for fever, systemic upset, trauma and the child’s age (see gait abnormalities)
🚩Always exclude septic arthritis
  • Febrile, will not weight-bear, holds the joint still, very tender → septic arthritis (see joint infection)
  • Kocher criteria: non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5°C, ESR >40, WCC >12 — more met = higher risk
  • Aspirate the joint and treat — the alternative (transient synovitis) is a diagnosis of exclusion
🟢Age 0–4 & 4–10
  • 0–4: DDH (waddling / limp, missed on screening), toddler’s fracture, non-accidental injury
  • 4–10: transient synovitis (post-viral, well / afebrile, weight-bears with a limp) — the commonest
  • Perthes (boys 4–8): avascular necrosis of the femoral head, insidious limp, reduced abduction / internal rotation (see paediatric orthopaedics)
🚩Age 10–16 — SUFE
  • Slipped upper femoral epiphysis: obese adolescent, often around the growth spurt; hip / thigh / knee pain
  • The leg lies externally rotated and shortened, with loss of internal rotation; confirm on a frog-leg lateral X-ray
  • Examine the hip in any child with knee pain — SUFE risks avascular necrosis and needs surgical pinning
🟣Don’t-miss & systemic
  • Non-accidental injury: inconsistent / changing history, delayed presentation, other bruises / fractures (see safeguarding)
  • Malignancy (leukaemia): night pain, pallor, bruising, hepatosplenomegaly, systemic upset (see paediatric cancers)
  • JIA: persistent arthritis >6 weeks, morning stiffness, a swollen joint (see JIA)
🩺Adults & investigation
  • Adult limp: osteoarthritis (hip / knee, see OA), fracture, lumbar radiculopathy, foot pathology, inflammatory arthritis
  • Child: FBC, CRP / ESR, blood cultures, X-ray (both hips, frog-leg for SUFE), ultrasound hip (effusion), and aspiration if septic
  • Apply Kocher to septic-vs-transient; a well, afebrile, weight-bearing child with normal bloods can often be observed

And knee pain in a child is a hip until proven otherwise.

MSK__Joint Swelling:
Joint swelling is worked up by what the swelling is made of — you decide this at the bedside by feel. There are four textures:
  • An effusion (fluid — fluctuant, with a patellar tap for a large knee effusion and a bulge / wipe test for a small one).
  • Synovial thickening (a boggy / doughy swelling of inflamed synovium — the hallmark of inflammatory arthritis).
  • Bony swelling (hard, from osteophytes — osteoarthritis, Heberden / Bouchard nodes).
  • Periarticular swelling (bursitis, a ganglion, a tophus, a Baker’s cyst or cellulitis — next to, not in, the joint).
  • The character of the swelling points straight to the diagnosis (see joint pain).
🚨A hot, red, tender effusion is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — aspirate before antibiotics (Gram / culture / crystals / cell count; see acute hot swollen joint, septic arthritis). A tense knee effusion after trauma suggests a haemarthrosis (ligament / fracture); lipohaemarthrosis (fat-fluid level) means an intra-articular fracture. A ruptured Baker’s cyst can mimic a DVT (calf pain and swelling; see Baker's cyst).

1Characterise the swelling
🔍Feel the swelling
  • Fluctuant → effusion (fluid); boggy / doughy → synovial thickening; hard → bony; next to the joint → periarticular
  • Note whether it is hot / red / tender (inflammatory / infective) or cool (mechanical)
  • Localise: is the swelling in the joint line (articular) or outside it (bursa, cyst, tophus)?
💧Prove an effusion
  • Patellar tap: empty the suprapatellar pouch, push the patella down — a “tap” = a large effusion
  • Bulge / wipe test: milk fluid across the joint line to show a fluid wave — detects a small effusion
  • Cross-fluctuation confirms fluid; an effusion is the sign that most often needs aspiration
🚩Hot effusion → aspirate
  • Hot, red, tender effusion = septic until proven otherwise → aspirate before antibiotics (see septic arthritis)
  • Send fluid for Gram stain, culture, crystals, cell count; take blood cultures (see hot joint)
  • Crystals → gout (negatively birefringent needles) / pseudogout (positively birefringent rhomboids, see crystal arthropathy); blood → haemarthrosis
🔵Synovial vs bony
  • Boggy, warm, symmetrical small-joint (MCP / PIP / wrist) synovial swelling → rheumatoid / inflammatory (see RA)
  • Hard, bony swelling with Heberden (DIP) and Bouchard (PIP) nodes, older, non-inflammatory → osteoarthritis (see OA)
  • Synovial thickening ≥ 6 weeks of an inflammatory arthritis needs early rheumatology referral
🟣Periarticular swellings
  • Bursitis (olecranon, prepatellar “housemaid’s knee”): fluctuant swelling over the bursa, joint moves freely (see bursitis)
  • Ganglion (firm cystic lump near a tendon / wrist), tophus (gout, see gouty tophi), rheumatoid nodule
  • Baker’s cyst: popliteal swelling; if it ruptures it mimics a DVT (see Baker's cyst)
🩺Investigate
  • Aspirate a significant / hot effusion (Gram / culture / crystals / cell count) — the decisive test
  • Ultrasound confirms an effusion / synovitis and guides aspiration; X-ray shows osteophytes, erosions, chondrocalcinosis
  • Bloods as directed: CRP / ESR, urate, RF / anti-CCP, and imaging (MRI) for the mass-like swellings
Name the texture, name the disease. Fluctuant = effusion (tap it, and if it is hot, aspirate it); boggy = synovitis (think inflammatory / rheumatoid); hard = bony (osteoarthritis); beside the joint = periarticular (bursa, ganglion, tophus, Baker’s cyst). The character of the swelling does most of the diagnostic work.

Effusion vs periarticular is “in vs beside” the joint. An effusion distends the whole joint line and gives a patellar tap / bulge; a bursitis, ganglion or cyst is a discrete swelling outside the joint, and the joint itself moves freely. That single distinction separates true arthritis from a periarticular lump.

MSK__Joint Stiffness:
Joint stiffness is sorted by one question: is it inflammatory or mechanical?
  • Inflammatory stiffness is early-morning stiffness (EMS) lasting >30–60 minutes that eases with activity and is worse after rest — the hallmark of rheumatoid arthritis, the spondyloarthropathies and polymyalgia rheumatica.
  • Mechanical stiffness is brief (<30 minutes), a short “gelling” after inactivity that soon wears off but is worse with use through the day — the pattern of osteoarthritis.
  • A third group is fixed loss of range — a frozen shoulder, an ankylosed (fused) joint, or a mechanically locked joint (see joint pain, joint swelling).
🚨Polymyalgia rheumatica overlaps with giant cell arteritis — new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual loss in a patient >50 with proximal girdle stiffness is GCA, a sight-threatening emergency needing immediate high-dose steroids (see polymyalgia / vasculitis). Persistent inflammatory stiffness (EMS >30 min for ≥6 weeks) needs early rheumatology referral before erosions form (see rheumatoid arthritis). Remember PMR is stiffness & pain with normal power (see muscle weakness).

1Split the stiffness
🔍Inflammatory or mechanical?
  • Inflammatory: EMS >30–60 min, eases with activity, worse after rest, ± swelling / systemic features
  • Mechanical: brief gelling <30 min after rest, worse with use through the day (see osteoarthritis)
  • Fixed loss of range: a globally stiff joint (frozen shoulder), a fused joint, or a locked one
🔵The inflammatory causes
  • Rheumatoid arthritis: symmetrical small-joint (MCP / PIP / wrist) EMS >1 hour (see RA)
  • Spondyloarthropathy: inflammatory back / buttock stiffness in the young, better with exercise (see spondyloarthropathy, back pain)
  • Polymyalgia rheumatica: proximal shoulder / hip-girdle stiffness, age >50, high ESR, normal power
🚩PMR → think GCA
  • PMR + new headache / scalp tenderness / jaw claudication / visual loss → giant cell arteritis (see vasculitis)
  • Sight-threatening emergency → immediate high-dose steroids and urgent temporal-artery assessment / biopsy
  • PMR itself responds dramatically to low-dose steroids — a poor response should make you doubt the diagnosis
🟢Mechanical / osteoarthritis
  • Brief gelling after rest that quickly frees up, then stiffness / pain worse with use later in the day
  • Older patient, large weight-bearing or DIP joints, bony swelling, normal inflammatory markers
  • No prolonged morning stiffness and no systemic features (see osteoarthritis)
🟣Fixed loss of range
  • Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis): global loss of active AND passive movement, especially external rotation; associated with diabetes (see shoulder disorders)
  • Ankylosis: a joint fused by advanced disease (e.g. AS spine, end-stage RA)
  • Locked / blocked joint: a mechanical block (meniscal tear, loose body) — sudden inability to fully extend
🩺Investigate by pattern
  • Inflammatory → CRP / ESR, RF / anti-CCP (RA), HLA-B27 selectively, imaging of hands / SI joints
  • PMR / GCA → ESR / CRP (usually high), and in GCA temporal-artery biopsy / ultrasound — do not delay steroids
  • Mechanical → usually clinical; X-ray for osteoarthritic change; frozen shoulder is a clinical diagnosis
Duration and direction split it. Inflammatory stiffness is long (>30–60 min) and eases with use; mechanical stiffness is brief and worse with use. That one contrast points you to RA / spondyloarthropathy / PMR on the inflammatory side or osteoarthritis on the mechanical side — and PMR should always make you screen for GCA.

MSK__Reduced Range of Movement / Joint D:
Reduced range of movement and a deformed joint are the visible end-points of joint disease.
  • The first bedside step is to compare active and passive movement: if active is limited but passive is full, the problem is in the muscle, tendon or nerve (a rotator-cuff tear, a tendon rupture, a nerve palsy); if both are limited, the problem is in the joint or capsule (arthritis, a frozen shoulder, or bony ankylosis).
  • Then read the deformity: the rheumatoid hand (ulnar deviation, swan-neck and boutonnière fingers, Z-thumb, subluxation) versus the osteoarthritic hand (Heberden / Bouchard nodes, squared thumb base) and limb malalignment (varus / valgus).
  • Deformity is fixed contracture, ankylosis or subluxation (see joint swelling, joint stiffness).
🚨A sudden loss of active movement after a pop or injury is a tendon rupture until proven otherwise — e.g. an Achilles rupture (positive Simmonds’ / calf-squeeze test), a ruptured long head of biceps or a rotator-cuff tear. A joint that is fixed, hot and will not move is septic arthritis (see joint pain). Sudden deformity after trauma may be a dislocation / fracture needing urgent reduction (check the distal neurovascular status; see dislocations).

1Localise & read the deformity
🔍Active vs passive range
  • Active limited, passive full → muscle / tendon / nerve problem (cuff tear, tendon rupture, palsy)
  • Both active and passive limited → joint / capsule problem (arthritis, frozen shoulder, ankylosis; see joint stiffness)
  • Compare with the other side and note whether movement is painful, blocked or fixed
🔵Causes of lost range
  • Pain / effusion (guarding), capsular contracture (frozen shoulder), ankylosis (bony fusion)
  • Mechanical block: a locked joint from a meniscal tear or loose body (sudden inability to fully extend)
  • Tendon rupture or nerve palsy (active loss), and fixed flexion deformity of chronic arthritis
🟢The rheumatoid hand
  • Ulnar deviation at the MCP joints and volar subluxation; symmetrical, with soft-tissue swelling (see RA)
  • Swan-neck = PIP hyper-extension + DIP flexion; boutonnière = PIP flexion + DIP hyper-extension
  • Z-shaped thumb, and later fixed deformities / ankylosis of long-standing disease
🟣OA & malalignment
  • Osteoarthritis: Heberden (DIP) and Bouchard (PIP) nodes, squaring of the thumb base (see OA)
  • Varus (bow-legged, medial-compartment knee OA) vs valgus (knock-kneed); hallux valgus (bunion, see foot & ankle)
  • Gouty tophi deform joints (see crystal arthropathy); a Charcot joint is grossly deformed but neuropathic (see Charcot joint)
🩹Contracture vs ankylosis vs subluxation
  • Contracture: soft-tissue shortening fixing the joint (Dupuytren’s, Volkmann’s ischaemic, burns; see hand & wrist)
  • Ankylosis: the joint is fused (fibrous or bony) by advanced disease — no movement at all
  • Subluxation / dislocation: joint surfaces partly / completely displaced — visible deformity (see dislocations)
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Measure the range (goniometer), note a fixed flexion deformity (e.g. hip — Thomas test) and the alignment
  • X-ray: erosions / joint-space loss, subluxation, alignment (varus / valgus), ankylosis, fracture / dislocation
  • Test the relevant tendon (e.g. Simmonds’ for Achilles) and nerve if active movement is selectively lost
Active vs passive is the master test. Active limited but passive full means the joint is fine — look at the tendon, muscle or nerve (a cuff tear or palsy). Both limited means the joint itself is the problem (arthritis, frozen shoulder, ankylosis). Then the pattern of deformity tells you rheumatoid (ulnar deviation, swan-neck / boutonnière) from osteoarthritis (nodes, varus knee).

MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump:
A soft-tissue lump is assessed in two moves. First, describe it systematically — site, size, shape, surface, consistency, fluctuance, transillumination, mobility, relation to deeper structures, skin change, temperature, tenderness and the regional lymph nodes. Second, and most important, screen for the “sarcoma” red flags: a lump that is >5 cm, deep to the fascia, rapidly growing, painful, or recurrent after excision must be referred urgently (2-week-wait) to a sarcoma centre. Most lumps are benign — a lipoma (soft, mobile, “slip sign”), a sebaceous cyst (skin-tethered punctum), a ganglion, a bursa, a rheumatoid nodule or a gouty tophus — but the job is to not miss the one that is not (see benign skin lumps, joint swelling).
🚨Refer urgently (2-week-wait) to a sarcoma service any soft-tissue lump that is >5 cm, deep to the deep fascia, increasing in size, painful or a recurrence — for MRI and image-guided core biopsy (see soft-tissue sarcoma / tumour). Never perform an unplanned local excision of a possible sarcoma (a “whoops procedure”) — it contaminates tissue planes and compromises limb-salvage surgery. A hot, tender, fluctuant lump with fever is an abscess needing drainage.

MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon:
Raynaud’s phenomenon is episodic vasospasm of the digital arteries, provoked by cold or emotion, producing the classic tricolour change: white (ischaemic pallor) → blue (cyanosis) → red (reactive hyperaemia on rewarming). The whole task is to decide whether it is primary (Raynaud’s disease — a benign, symmetrical vasospasm in a young woman with no underlying disease) or secondary (Raynaud’s phenomenon — a marker of an underlying disorder, above all a connective-tissue disease such as systemic sclerosis; see connective tissue disease). A handful of red flags — older onset, asymmetry, digital ulcers, abnormal nailfold capillaries and a positive ANA — separate the two (see joint pain).
🚨A digit that stays white / dusky, painful and does not reperfuse, or develops ulceration or gangrene, is critical digital ischaemia — an emergency needing urgent rheumatology / vascular referral and often an IV prostacyclin (iloprost) infusion (see connective tissue disease). New Raynaud’s with digital pitting scars, sclerodactyly or telangiectasia points to systemic sclerosis. Always ask about a beta-blocker and about hand-transmitted vibration at work.

  • Connective-tissue disease: systemic sclerosis (the key one), SLE, dermatomyositis (see muscle weakness), MCTD, Sjögren’s (see connective tissue disease)

MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheumatic Di:
The nails and skin are a window onto rheumatic disease. A joint complaint is often solved by looking at the hands: nail pitting and onycholysis point to psoriatic arthritis; dilated nailfold capillaries to scleroderma or dermatomyositis; and nailfold infarcts or splinter haemorrhages to a vasculitis. The skin adds the rest: a psoriasis plaque, a malar or heliotrope rash, sclerodactyly and telangiectasia, palpable purpura, rheumatoid nodules or gouty tophi each name the underlying disease. This topic is pattern recognition — matching a cutaneous sign to its rheumatological diagnosis (see polyarthritis, Raynaud's).
🚨Palpable purpura, nailfold infarcts, splinter haemorrhages and digital gangrene are signs of an active vasculitis — which can threaten organs (kidney, lung, nerve) and needs urgent assessment and immunosuppression (see vasculitis). In an adult, dermatomyositis (heliotrope rash, Gottron’s papules) is paraneoplastic until proven otherwise — screen for malignancy (see connective tissue disease). New digital pitting scars or ulcers with Raynaud’s point to systemic sclerosis.

MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pain:
Chronic widespread pain — pain in multiple regions on both sides, above and below the waist, for >3 months — has one central diagnosis: fibromyalgia.
  • Fibromyalgia is a disorder of amplified central pain processing (“nociplastic” pain); its signature is widespread pain, profound fatigue, non-restorative sleep and cognitive slowing (“fibro-fog”), often with headaches, irritable bowel and low mood.
  • The defining feature at the bedside is what is normal: no synovitis, a normal examination, and normal inflammatory markers and investigations.
  • The whole skill is to exclude the organic mimics — inflammatory arthritis, PMR, hypothyroidism, osteomalacia, lupus — before making this clinical diagnosis (see fibromyalgia, joint pain).
🚨Fibromyalgia is a diagnosis made after excluding organic disease — do not attach the label in the presence of red flags: weight loss, fever, night sweats, focal or objective signs (synovitis, weakness, rash), or raised inflammatory markers. A high ESR / CRP is never fibromyalgia — think inflammatory arthritis, PMR (see vasculitis / PMR) or malignancy. Always check TFTs and calcium / vitamin D (hypothyroidism, osteomalacia) before settling on the diagnosis.

  • Widespread pain + profound fatigue + non-restorative (unrefreshing) sleep + cognitive “fibro-fog”
  • Frequent overlaps: tension headaches, irritable bowel, low mood / anxiety, paraesthesiae
  • Classic tender points at defined sites; newer criteria use a widespread-pain index + symptom-severity score (see fibromyalgia)

  • Normal joint examination — no synovitis, no swelling, full range of movement, normal power
  • Normal inflammatory markers (CRP / ESR) and normal routine bloods — investigations are done to exclude, not confirm
  • A clinical diagnosis: the pattern + normal exam + normal bloods, once mimics are excluded

  • Inflammatory arthritis / connective-tissue disease: synovitis, high CRP, autoantibodies (see rheumatoid arthritis, connective tissue disease)

  • Fibromyalgia is nociplastic pain — amplified central pain processing, not tissue damage or nerve injury

MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis:
Enthesitis and dactylitis are the two signs that shout spondyloarthropathy. Enthesitis is inflammation at an enthesis — where a tendon, ligament or capsule inserts into bone — classically the Achilles insertion and the plantar fascia (heel pain), the patellar tendon and the iliac crest. Dactylitis (a “sausage digit”) is diffuse swelling of an entire finger or toe, combining synovitis + tenosynovitis + enthesitis. Both point away from rheumatoid arthritis (which is a synovitis) and toward a seronegative spondyloarthropathy — psoriatic, reactive, ankylosing or enteropathic arthritis, linked to HLA-B27 (see spondyloarthropathy, polyarthritis).
🚨A single hot, exquisitely tender, sausage-swollen finger held in flexion may be an infective flexor tenosynovitis — a surgical emergency. Look for the four Kanavel signs: fusiform swelling, finger held flexed, tenderness along the flexor sheath, and pain on passive extension → urgent hand-surgery referral and washout (see bone & joint infection). Also exclude gout (see crystal arthropathy) and, in a child, sickle-cell dactylitis.

MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Tenderness:
Jaw claudication (aching in the jaw / cheek that builds while chewing and eases on stopping) and scalp tenderness (pain combing the hair or resting the head on a pillow) in a patient over 50 are the alarm signs of giant cell (temporal) arteritis — a large-vessel vasculitis and an ophthalmic emergency (see vasculitis). The whole point of the topic is a single reflex: recognise the cluster (new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, a tender or pulseless temporal artery, raised ESR / CRP, often with polymyalgia rheumatica overlap, see joint stiffness) and start high-dose corticosteroids immediately — before the biopsy — because the threatened complication is sudden, irreversible blindness from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (see acute painless visual loss). Jaw claudication is the most specific symptom and, with any visual symptom, marks the highest risk.
🚨Visual loss in GCA is sudden and permanent — act before the biopsy. Amaurosis fugax, diplopia or any transient visual blurring in a patient with these symptoms means ischaemia at the optic nerve head is imminent (see amaurosis fugax, diplopia). Once one eye is lost the fellow eye can follow within days. Start corticosteroids the moment GCA is suspected — IV methylprednisolone if there are any visual symptoms, otherwise oral prednisolone 40–60 mg; add aspirin and gastro / bone protection, and arrange temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound urgently (steroids do not negate a biopsy done within 1–2 weeks). Do not wait for the ESR to come back to treat.

🚩Recognise the GCA cluster
  • Age >50 (usually >60) with a new headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication (the most specific symptom)
  • Temporal artery thickened, tender, nodular or pulseless; may have visual or constitutional features

  • Amaurosis fugax or transient blurring → warning of imminent anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (see amaurosis fugax)

  • Diplopia from extra-ocular muscle ischaemia; the fellow eye can be lost within days if untreated (see diplopia)

  • Polymyalgia rheumatica in up to half: shoulder & hip-girdle pain / stiffness, worse in the morning (see joint stiffness)

  • Large-vessel disease: limb claudication, bruits, and later aortic aneurysm / dissection
🚩Treat before you confirm
  • Start steroids the moment GCA is suspected — do not wait for ESR or biopsy

  • Jaw pain on chewing: temporomandibular joint dysfunction or dental disease (pain at the joint / tooth, not ischaemic fatigue)

  • ESR / CRP / plasma viscosity urgently; FBC (normocytic anaemia, thrombocytosis)
  • Temporal artery biopsy (long segment — skip lesions) and / or temporal artery ultrasound (halo sign)

MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotated Leg:
A shortened and externally rotated leg in an older person who has fallen and cannot weight-bear is a fractured neck of femur until proven otherwise (see lower limb fractures, hip pain). The displaced proximal fragment is pulled up and rotated out by the iliopsoas and short external rotators, giving the classic posture; the hip is painful to move and the leg looks short. The key anatomical split is intracapsular vs extracapsular, because an intracapsular fracture can strip the femoral head’s blood supply and cause avascular necrosis (see AVN) — which is why displaced intracapsular fractures are usually replaced (hemiarthroplasty / total hip) while extracapsular ones are fixed (dynamic hip screw / nail). Most are fragility fractures in osteoporotic bone (see metabolic bone disease); always ask why they fell.
🚨Treat the patient, not just the hip. A hip fracture is a major physiological insult in a frail patient: give prompt analgesia (consider a fascia iliaca block), resuscitate, screen for the cause of the fall (arrhythmia, sepsis, stroke, medication, hypoglycaemia), and check for anaemia / dehydration / AKI. Aim for surgery within 36 hours on an orthogeriatric pathway — delay increases mortality. Do not be reassured by a normal X-ray: an occult fracture with ongoing pain and inability to weight-bear needs an MRI. Beware the mimic — a posterior hip dislocation gives a shortened, INTERNALLY rotated, adducted leg (see dislocations) — and watch for fat embolism after long-bone injury (see fat embolism).

🚩Recognise the fracture
  • Fallen older patient, can’t weight-bear, leg short + externally rotated, hip painful on any movement / axial load

  • Intracapsular (subcapital / transcervical): risks the femoral-head blood supply → avascular necrosis / non-union (see AVN)
  • Extracapsular (intertrochanteric / subtrochanteric): blood supply preserved — fix rather than replace
  • Garden classification grades intracapsular displacement (I–IV) and guides replace-vs-fix
🩺The operation follows the anatomy
  • Displaced intracapsular → replace: total hip (fitter / active) or hemiarthroplasty (less mobile)
  • Undisplaced intracapsular → internal fixation (cannulated screws) in selected patients
  • Extracapsular → dynamic hip screw (intertrochanteric) or intramedullary nail (subtrochanteric / reverse-oblique)

  • Analgesia early — consider a fascia iliaca block; resuscitate, correct anaemia / dehydration / AKI

  • Consider fragility-fracture work-up: bone health, falls assessment, osteoporosis treatment (see metabolic bone disease)

MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain):
Sciatica is radicular leg pain — a sharp, shooting, often electric pain that travels down the leg below the knee in the territory of a lumbosacral nerve root (usually L5 or S1), commonly with paraesthesia and sometimes weakness. The commonest cause is a prolapsed intervertebral disc compressing the root; also lateral / foraminal stenosis, spondylolisthesis, and (rarely) tumour or infection (see radiculopathy). The first skill is to separate true radicular pain (dermatomal, below the knee, positive nerve-tension tests) from referred somatic back / buttock pain (dull, above the knee, no dermatome, see back pain). Most sciatica settles conservatively; image and refer only for red flags or a persistent / severe deficit. The one emergency to screen for every time is cauda equina syndrome (see lower back & spine).
🚨Screen every sciatica for cauda equina syndrome. Bilateral sciatica, saddle (perineal) anaesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction (retention with overflow, incontinence), reduced anal tone or sexual dysfunction mean cauda equina compression → emergency whole-spine MRI and surgical decompression — delay causes permanent bladder / bowel and sexual damage (see cauda equina). A progressive or severe motor deficit (e.g. a new foot drop) also needs urgent referral (see foot drop). Night pain, weight loss or a cancer history suggests malignant root compression (see bone tumours); fever, IV drug use or immunosuppression suggests discitis / epidural abscess (see spinal infection).

MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot:
A hot, red, swollen foot in a patient with peripheral neuropathy (usually diabetic) poses one pivotal question: is this acute Charcot neuroarthropathy or infection (cellulitis / osteomyelitis / septic arthritis)? They look almost identical, but the management diverges completely — Charcot is offloaded, infection is treated with antibiotics ± surgery — and both are limb-threatening if missed (see Charcot joint, bone & joint infection). The discriminators are a portal of entry (an ulcer or skin break favours infection; intact skin favours Charcot), systemic upset (fever, raised inflammatory markers favour infection), and the elevation test (erythema that fades on elevating the leg favours Charcot; erythema that persists favours infection). Remember the neuropathic foot usually has bounding pulses — this is a warm, well-perfused problem, not an ischaemic one. Also consider gout, DVT and fracture.
🚨A missed acute Charcot foot collapses. Untreated, the neuropathic bones fragment and dislocate into a rocker-bottom deformity that ulcerates and can cost the limb — so a hot, swollen, >2°C warmer foot in a neuropathic patient is Charcot until proven otherwise: offload immediately (total-contact cast), non-weight-bear and refer to the diabetic-foot MDT the same day, even if the X-ray is normal (early changes show only on MRI as marrow oedema, see Charcot). On the infection side, an ulcer that probes to bone is osteomyelitis; treat sepsis, and beware necrotising fasciitis — pain out of proportion, crepitus, rapidly spreading dusky skin and systemic collapse — a surgical emergency. Charcot and infection can coexist.

MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Achilles):
Simmonds’ test (the Thompson or calf-squeeze test) screens for a complete Achilles tendon rupture. Position the patient prone with the feet hanging over the end of the couch (or kneeling on a chair) and squeeze the calf (gastrocnemius–soleus). Normally this plantarflexes the foot; if the tendon is ruptured, the squeeze is not transmitted and the foot does not move — a positive test. It is the single most useful bedside sign because a patient with a full rupture can often still weakly plantarflex using other muscles, so preserved active movement does not exclude it (see foot & ankle disorders). Confirm with the palpable gap and Matles test, and remember the fluoroquinolone / steroid association.

🔍How to elicit it
  • Patient prone, feet over the end of the couch (or kneeling on a chair) with the calves relaxed
  • Squeeze the calf (gastrocnemius–soleus) firmly and watch the foot
  • Normal = the foot plantarflexes; positive = the foot stays still (no plantarflexion)

  • A complete Achilles tendon rupture — the calf squeeze can no longer be transmitted to the foot
  • Squeezing bunches the muscle but the divided tendon does not pull the heel
  • Compare with the other leg, which should plantarflex normally

  • Palpable gap in the tendon, usually 2–6 cm above the insertion (the watershed zone)
  • Matles test: prone knee flexion to 90° — the ruptured foot falls into neutral / dorsiflexion while the normal foot stays plantarflexed
  • Increased resting dorsiflexion from loss of tendon tone

  • Typical: a sudden pop / feeling of being “kicked” during push-off in a middle-aged athlete (racquet / court sports)
  • Risk factors: fluoroquinolone antibiotics, corticosteroids, gout, chronic tendinopathy

Because a full rupture can still allow weak active plantarflexion, preserved movement does not exclude it — trust the squeeze test, the gap and Matles.

MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Quervain's):
Finkelstein’s test is the bedside test for De Quervain’s tenosynovitis — a stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment of the wrist, which carries the abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) tendons over the radial styloid. Ask the patient to tuck the thumb into the palm and make a fist over it, then ulnar-deviate the wrist (or grasp the thumb and pull it into ulnar deviation): sharp pain over the radial styloid is a positive test. It localises pain to the APL / EPB tendons rather than the joint, and its classic patients are new mothers (“mummy thumb”) and anyone with repetitive thumb / wrist use (see hand & wrist disorders). Distinguish it from thumb-base (1st CMC) osteoarthritis and a scaphoid fracture (see Tinel, Phalen).

MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip):
Trendelenburg’s sign tests the hip abductor mechanism — the gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve, L4–S1) that hold the pelvis level when you stand on one leg. Ask the patient to stand on one leg: normally the abductors of the stance leg contract and the opposite (lifted) side of the pelvis rises or stays level. If that mechanism fails, the pelvis drops on the side of the lifted leg — a positive sign. The crucial rule is that the pelvis sags on the side opposite the weak hip — “sound side sags”. It reflects a problem with the nerve, the muscle, the joint (pain) or the bony fulcrum of the stance hip, and on walking it produces a Trendelenburg (waddling) gait (see hip pain, limp).

MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakness):
Gower’s sign is a child climbing up their own body to stand from the floor. With weak pelvic-girdle muscles — the hip extensors (gluteus maximus) and knee extensors (quadriceps) — they cannot rise directly, so they turn prone, push up onto hands and feet, and “walk” their hands up their thighs to lever themselves upright. It is the classic bedside sign of proximal lower-limb weakness and, in a young boy, strongly suggests Duchenne muscular dystrophy (see muscular dystrophies) — but it appears in any proximal myopathy (see proximal muscle weakness). The single most useful next test is a creatine kinase, which is markedly raised in muscular dystrophy.

🔍How to elicit it
  • Ask the child to get up from lying / sitting on the floor to standing and watch how they do it
  • Positive: they turn prone, push up into a “bear” position (hands and feet down), then “walk” the hands up the thighs
  • They are climbing up their own body because they cannot straighten the hips and knees against gravity
🧒What a positive sign means
  • Proximal lower-limb (pelvic-girdle) weakness — weak hip and knee extensors
  • Classic for Duchenne muscular dystrophy in a young boy, but not specific to it

🔵The Duchenne picture
  • Boy, 3–5 years: delayed walking, waddling gait, frequent falls, calf pseudohypertrophy
  • X-linked recessive (dystrophin gene); markedly raised CK; confirm with genetic testing ± muscle biopsy
  • Progressive — wheelchair by early teens, with cardiomyopathy and respiratory decline (see muscular dystrophies)
🟣Broader causes
  • Becker muscular dystrophy: similar but milder / later; other congenital or metabolic myopathies
  • Spinal muscular atrophy and other paediatric neuromuscular disease (see paediatric neuromuscular)
  • Inflammatory myopathy (juvenile dermatomyositis — rash + weakness); in adults, any proximal myopathy (see proximal muscle weakness)
Walking the hands up the legs to stand = proximal weakness. Gower’s sign reflects weak hip and knee extensors. In a young boy with calf pseudohypertrophy it is Duchenne muscular dystrophy until a CK and genetics say otherwise — but any proximal myopathy can produce it.

MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Impingemen:
The painful arc is a bedside test for subacromial impingement. Ask the patient to abduct the arm through its full range: pain that appears in the mid-arc, roughly 60–120°, and eases above and below it, is a positive sign. In this zone the greater tuberosity and the supraspinatus tendon / subacromial bursa are compressed under the acromion and coraco-acromial arch. A positive arc points to rotator-cuff tendinopathy / subacromial impingement (see shoulder disorders, shoulder pain). Note the height of the pain: a high arc above ~160° instead localises to the acromioclavicular joint, and pain with weakness and a positive drop-arm means a cuff tear, not simple impingement.

  • Ask the patient to actively abduct the arm from the side up to overhead, then lower it

MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supraspinatu:
The empty-can (Jobe) test isolates the supraspinatus, the rotator-cuff muscle most often torn. Position the arm at 90° of abduction in the scapular plane (about 30° forward of the coronal plane) with the thumb pointing down — as if emptying a can — and press down against the patient’s resistance. Pain or weakness is a positive test, pointing to supraspinatus tendinopathy or a tear (see shoulder disorders, shoulder pain). The key discrimination is pain vs weakness: pain suggests tendinopathy / impingement (pair it with the painful arc), while marked weakness with a positive drop-arm suggests a full-thickness tear. If the empty-can position is too painful, the gentler full-can (thumb-up) variant tests the same muscle.

MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical Presen:
A fracture presents with pain, swelling, deformity and loss of function, and on examination focal bony tenderness, abnormal mobility and crepitus (do not deliberately elicit these). The clinical task has three parts: recognise it, describe it (bone, site, pattern, displacement, and open vs closed), and — most importantly — find the emergencies. Every fractured limb needs a neurovascular assessment (pulses, capillary refill, sensation, movement) before and after any manipulation, and a deliberate search for an open fracture and compartment syndrome. Major trauma is managed by an ATLS primary survey (ABCDE + C-spine) first — life before limb (see bone pain, reduced range / deformity).
🚨Open (compound) fracture = bone / haematoma communicates with a wound → emergency: photograph, remove gross contamination, cover with a saline-soaked dressing, IV antibiotics + tetanus, analgesia, realign & splint, and urgent orthopaedic / plastics referral (see lower-limb fractures). Compartment syndrome = pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch → emergency fasciotomy (the pulseless ‘Ps’ are late; see compartment syndrome). Always document the distal neurovascular status.

1Recognise, describe, find emergencies
🔍Recognise a fracture
  • Pain, swelling, deformity, loss of function, and focal bony tenderness over the injury
  • Abnormal mobility and crepitus (a bony grating) — do not deliberately elicit these
  • Note the mechanism (high vs low energy) and screen for other injuries (major trauma → ATLS ABCDE first)
📐Describe the fracture
  • Which bone and site (proximal / shaft / distal, intra- vs extra-articular)
  • Pattern: transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, segmental, greenstick (children)
  • Displacement (translation, angulation, rotation, shortening) and open vs closed
🚩Open fracture — emergency
  • Bone / fracture haematoma communicates with a wound (compound) — high infection risk (see upper-limb fractures)
  • Photograph, remove gross debris, cover with saline-soaked gauze, IV antibiotics + tetanus, analgesia, realign & splint
  • Urgent orthopaedics / plastics; graded by the Gustilo-Anderson classification
🚩Neurovascular check & compartment syndrome
  • Assess pulses, capillary refill, sensation and movement distal to the fracture — before and after reduction
  • Compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch → urgent fasciotomy (see compartment syndrome)
  • The classic late ‘Ps’ (pulseless, pallor, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishingly cold) are a late vascular picture (see cold leg)
🟣Systemic & early complications
  • Haemorrhage / shock: femur (~1–1.5 L) and pelvic fractures bleed heavily — resuscitate (see lower-limb fractures)
  • Fat embolism syndrome (long-bone / pelvic): respiratory distress, petechiae, confusion at 24–72 h (see fat embolism)
  • VTE risk; and later non-union, malunion, avascular necrosis, infection
🟢Special fractures & patterns
  • Fragility fracture: low-energy fall in osteoporosis → assess bone health (see metabolic bone disease)
  • Pathological fracture: through abnormal bone (metastasis / myeloma; see bone tumours); stress fracture in athletes
  • Children: greenstick and Salter-Harris (physeal) fractures (see paediatric fractures); consider non-accidental injury (see safeguarding)

In major trauma, ATLS ABCDE comes before the limb.

MSK__Tinel's Sign:
Tinel’s sign is a bedside test for an irritable peripheral nerve: lightly percussing over the nerve reproduces tingling / “pins-and-needles” (paraesthesiae) shooting into that nerve’s sensory distribution. It is positive when the tapping recreates the patient’s symptoms distally. Its most common use is carpal tunnel syndrome — tapping the median nerve at the wrist produces tingling in the thumb, index, middle and radial-half of the ring finger (the radial 3½ digits; see compression neuropathies). The same principle localises cubital-tunnel (ulnar at the elbow) and tarsal-tunnel compression, and tracks a regenerating nerve after repair (see Phalen's test, sensory disturbance).

1Elicit & interpret
🔍How to elicit it
  • Lightly tap / percuss over the course of the nerve (e.g. with a finger or tendon hammer)
  • Positive = tingling / electric paraesthesiae shooting distally into the nerve’s sensory territory, reproducing symptoms
  • At the wrist it tests the median nerve (carpal tunnel); it is a test of an irritable / regenerating nerve
🖐️What a positive test means
  • Median at the wrist → carpal tunnel syndrome: tingling in the radial 3½ digits (see compression neuropathies)
  • Ulnar at the elbow (cubital tunnel) → tingling in the little and ring fingers
  • Posterior tibial at the ankle (tarsal tunnel) → tingling in the sole
🔵Carpal tunnel context
  • Median nerve compressed under the flexor retinaculum; nocturnal tingling, relieved by shaking the hand
  • Risk factors: pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid, obesity, repetitive use, acromegaly
  • Later: thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction; confirm with nerve conduction studies if needed
🟣Interpret with care
  • Tinel’s is fairly specific but not very sensitive — a negative test does not exclude entrapment
  • Use it alongside Phalen’s test and the history (see Phalen's test)
  • An advancing Tinel’s down a nerve after repair signals axonal regeneration (see peripheral nerve injuries)

MSK__Phalen's Test:
Phalen’s test is a bedside provocation test for carpal tunnel syndrome: the patient holds the wrists in full flexion (backs of the hands pressed together, elbows out) for about 60 seconds. It is positive when this reproduces tingling / paraesthesiae in the median-nerve territory — the thumb, index, middle and radial-half of the ring finger (the radial 3½ digits). Sustained flexion raises pressure in the carpal tunnel and squeezes the already-irritable median nerve (see compression neuropathies). It is the natural partner to Tinel’s sign and is generally the more sensitive of the two (see Tinel's sign, sensory disturbance).

MSK__Froment's Sign:
Froment’s sign is a bedside test for ulnar-nerve palsy. Ask the patient to grip a sheet of paper between the thumb and the side of the index finger and hold on as you pull it away. Normally the adductor pollicis (an ulnar-innervated thumb muscle) keeps the thumb flat. If it is weak, the patient compensates by flexing the thumb’s interphalangeal (IP) joint using flexor pollicis longus (median / anterior interosseous) to grip — a positive sign. It localises an ulnar lesion (elbow / cubital tunnel or wrist / Guyon’s canal; see compression neuropathies) and complements the median-nerve tests (see Tinel's sign, Phalen's test).

1Elicit & interpret
🔍How to elicit it
  • Ask the patient to hold a sheet of paper between the thumb and the side of the index finger; try to pull it out
  • Positive = the thumb IP joint flexes to grip (flexor pollicis longus compensating) instead of staying flat
  • It tests adductor pollicis — an ulnar-innervated muscle of the thumb
✋What a positive test means
  • Ulnar-nerve palsy — weakness of adductor pollicis (the muscle Froment’s specifically tests)
  • Look also for Jeanne’s sign: compensatory hyperextension of the thumb MCP joint
  • Fits with wasting of the interossei / hypothenar muscles and an ulnar claw hand
🔵Where the ulnar nerve is trapped
  • Elbow / cubital tunnel (most common) — often with elbow pain and little/ring-finger tingling
  • Wrist / Guyon’s canal — e.g. cyclists, ganglion; may spare the dorsal sensory branch
  • A higher (elbow) lesion paradoxically gives a less clawed hand (the “ulnar paradox”)
🟣Interpret with care
  • Confirms weak thumb adduction, not the site — localise with the history, sensory pattern and Tinel’s
  • Test both hands and compare; look for interossei weakness (finger abduction/adduction)
  • Confirm and localise the lesion with nerve conduction studies where needed (see peripheral nerve injuries)
Thumb bends to hold the paper. Froment’s sign is positive when a weak adductor pollicis (ulnar) forces the patient to flex the thumb IP joint (flexor pollicis longus, median) to keep hold. It signals an ulnar-nerve palsy — pair it with Jeanne’s sign (MCP hyperextension).
